source: "State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025" (the 2025 DORA Report), DORA / Google Cloud; PDF version v. 2025.2 (142 pages, PDF created 15 Oct 2025). Chapter authors include Nathen Harvey (DORA Lead), Derek DeBellis, Kevin M. Storer, Daniella Villalba; premier research partner IT Revolution; research partners GitHub, GitLab, SkillBench, Workhelix. Companion announcement: "Announcing the 2025 DORA Report: State of AI-Assisted Software Development", Google Cloud blog, Nathen Harvey and Derek DeBellis, September 24, 2025. URLs opened: https://dora.dev/research/2025/dora-report/ ; https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_state_of_ai_assisted_software_development.pdf ; https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report
data_type: Survey (cross-sectional, analysed with Bayesian models and DAG-based confounder adjustment; effects reported as standardised coefficients with 89% credible intervals), supplemented by 78 qualitative interviews.
sample_and_method: "This year, a total of 4,867 respondents answered our survey." Global survey "conducted between June 13 and July 21, 2025", localised into English, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Japanese and Simplified Chinese. Recruitment: organic (blog posts, email campaigns, social media, snowball sampling) supplemented by a panel aimed at under-represented groups and industries; the report says organic responses alone were sufficient. Respondents were randomly assigned to one of four overlapping survey flows (AI, platform engineering, sociocognitive aspects, AI capabilities), so not every respondent answered every question. Interviews: 78 participants, July 2024 to July 2025, about 90 minutes each, remote. Respondents: median age 41; 62.8% men, 19.2% women; most common roles full-stack developer 15.0%, engineering manager 9.3%, back-end developer 9.3%; senior executives 4.2%; median six years in role. AI adoption is a latent factor built from three items: reliance, trust and reflexive use.
vendor_interest: Yes. Published by Google Cloud (sells Gemini and AI tooling); sponsors and research partners include GitHub and GitLab (AI coding tools), SkillBench and Workhelix (AI measurement/adoption tooling). The blog post page carries a "Try Gemini today" promotion.
headline_figures: (1) "Ninety percent of this year's survey respondents report using AI at work, a 14.1% increase over the same metric in last year's report." (2) "More than 80% of this year's survey respondents report a perception that AI has increased their productivity. Although more than 40% report that their productivity has increased only 'slightly,' fewer than 10% of respondents perceive AI contributing to any decrease in their productivity." (chart: 13% extremely, 31% moderately, 41% slightly increased; 9% no impact). (3) "a majority (59%) of survey respondents also observe that AI has positively impacted their code quality." (4) Trust: "While 30% of those surveyed indicate a more reserved stance, with 'a little' (23%) or 'no trust at all' (7%) in the quality of AI-generated output"; 70% have some confidence, "nearly a quarter of respondents (24%) who report having 'a great deal' or 'a lot' of trust." (5) "Survey respondents report spending a median of two hours of their most recent workday interacting with AI, representing about one-quarter of an eight-hour workday." (6) Experience: "a median of 16 months and a mean of 16.22 months of experience." (7) "Among AI users, only 7% report 'always' using AI when faced with a problem to solve or a task to complete, while 39% only 'sometimes' seek AI for help." (8) "Daily use is also common, with 47% of respondents using AI tools every day." (9) Agents: "a majority (61%) of respondents reporting 'never' interacting with AI tools in an agentic mode." (10) "the number one use for AI tools among this year's survey respondents is writing new code, with 71% of respondents who write code using AI to assist them in doing so." (11) Outcomes: "the person with higher AI adoption will report: Higher levels of individual effectiveness; Higher levels of software delivery instability; Higher levels of organizational performance; A higher percentage of time doing valuable work; Higher levels of code quality; Higher levels of product performance; Higher levels of software delivery throughput; Higher levels of team performance; Similar levels of burnout; Similar levels of friction." (12) Restated from DORA 2024: "an estimated 1.5% reduction in software delivery throughput and an estimated 7.2% increase in software delivery instability for every 25% increase in AI adoption." (13) Restated from METR: "developers who were slowed down by AI tools by 19% still believed the tools had made them 20% more efficient." (14) "90% of organizations have adopted platform engineering." (15) Blog: "However, skepticism remains as 30% report little or no trust in the code generated by AI, a slightly lower percentage than last year but a key trend to note." The standardised effect sizes in Figure 28 are shown only on a chart (axis -0.05 to 0.20); the report text does not print the coefficients, so exact magnitudes are not given here.
metric_layer: Input/usage: AI adoption factor (reliance, trust, reflexive use), time with AI, task use, interaction mode. Activity/perceived output: individual effectiveness (self-assessed; called "productivity" in 2024), valuable work, perceived productivity and code quality. Delivery: software delivery throughput (lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, rework rate), both self-reported in the survey. Quality: code quality, product performance. Organisational: organizational performance (self-reported profitability, market share, customer satisfaction). Wellbeing: burnout, friction. No direct financial outcome is measured.
respondent_role_split: Not given for the AI findings. The report publishes the role distribution of respondents (full-stack 15.0%, engineering manager 9.3%, back-end 9.3%, senior executive 4.2%, etc.) but does not split adoption, productivity or trust figures by IC, manager or executive. The adoption measure was deliberately designed so it "shouldn't be biased toward any single role".
workload_signal: Median two hours a day interacting with AI. No relationship between AI adoption and burnout or friction. On friction: "For an individual, friction doesn't vanish so much as move: It shifts from manual grind to deciding and verifying, possibly in the form of prompt iteration, result vetting, and assessing code that looks remarkably similar to correct code." On intensification: "some clear signals are emerging from our qualitative work which are aligned with literature on work intensification, suggesting perceived capacity gains from AI-assisted development tools have invited higher expectations of work output in some organizations." Interviewee: "Stakeholders are expecting more work to be done within [the product] in a quicker manner. So deadlines and projects are on a shorter time crunch". Pressure to adopt: 2024 interviewees described "fear of missing out" and "getting left behind". No hours-worked or time-correcting-AI figures.
definition_of_value_offered: Partly. The report frames value as organisational, not tool-level: "The greatest returns on AI investment come not from the tools themselves, but from a strategic focus on the underlying organizational system." It measures value across ten outcomes (above) and warns that "Widespread adoption doesn't automatically equal widespread value." The Metrics frameworks chapter tells organisations to define the goals and decisions measurement will inform, pick a framework (SPACE, DevEx, HEART, DORA delivery metrics), add AI-specific measures such as suggestion acceptance rate and trust while keeping existing baselines, and follow Plan-Do-Check-Adjust. It does not define ROI or financial payback. Closing line: "The greatest risk in this evolving landscape isn't falling behind, but rather investing heavily in chaotic activity that fails to deliver meaningful results."
removal_counterfactual: No direct evidence. All findings are between-person comparisons of higher vs lower AI adoption at one point in time. The ownership analysis compares AI vs no-AI responses ("78% certainty that AI adoption is not associated with developers feeling a diminished sense of personal ownership"). The report cites the METR RCT (19% slower, believed 20% faster) as evidence of a perception gap, but runs no withdrawal or control-group study.
key_quotes: 1) "AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there." (Google Cloud blog, 24 Sep 2025) 2) "instability still has significant detrimental effects on crucial outcomes like product performance and burnout, which can ultimately negate any perceived gains in throughput." (report, p. 41)
caveats: Self-reported survey data throughout, including the delivery metrics; productivity and code quality figures are explicitly perceptions. Cross-sectional: the authors say "we will speak in terms of comparisons" and "we don't want to give false assurances that we understand the underlying causal structure." Sample is self-selected via DORA's channels plus a panel, and respondents were split across four flows, so per-question n is below 4,867 (not stated per figure). Effect sizes are small standardised coefficients (all under 0.2 on the chart). Trust, reliance and reflexive use are folded into one adoption factor, so "higher adoption" partly means "higher trust". Vendor-sponsored. Cross-write-up differences: the report says a "14.1% increase" in AI use; the blog says trust scepticism is "slightly lower ... than last year", which I did not check against the 2024 report [uncertain]; the tokenmaxxing post restates the 30% low-trust figure as "developers" though it covers all respondents; the ROI report describes the instability effect as "second largest", read from the chart ordering. The 2024 comparison figures (1.5%, 7.2%) and the METR figures are restated, not re-checked against their primaries.
access: Primary opened in full but read selectively: the 142-page PDF (v. 2025.2) was downloaded and text-extracted; I read the executive summary, foreword, AI adoption and use, Exploring AI's relationship to key outcomes, sociocognitive impact, Metrics frameworks, Final thoughts, and parts of Demographics and Methodology. Not read in full: DORA AI Capabilities Model, Platform engineering, Value stream management, The AI mirror, and the research model chapters. Landing page and Google Cloud blog post opened in full (blog quotes checked against raw HTML). Not verified: the DORA 2024 report figures and METR study figures it restates.
